Renato, you have sixty seconds. Imagine I am a director from another country, and we meet at the coffee break. Go.
Hi, I'm Renato Annunciato. I am the commercial manager for the South and Southeast at Ipsen Brazil.
That is your job title. Everybody in the room has one. Where is your hook?
OK. Last year, a small regional team of seven consultants grew market share by three percentage points. I lead that team.
Now you stand out. Why should I remember your team, and not the others?
Our unique selling point is the relationship. We visit the key doctors in person every month, and we tailor every visit to the clinic.
Good. Keep it concise, though. One sentence is enough. And what do you want from me?
I would like to share our long-term plan for the interior of Sao Paulo with your team.
That is a call to action, but make it small and clear. What exactly is the next step?
Could I send you the plan by email tomorrow, and we talk for thirty minutes next week?
Perfect. Hook, who you are, what is different, and the ask. Fifty-five seconds, and memorable.

At a big global meeting, about twenty or thirty people introduce themselves to me during the coffee breaks. I am happy to meet them, but by the evening I remember maybe three. So I want to tell you what the forgettable ones do. The first mistake is the job title. A person says, I am the commercial manager for this or that region, and stops. That tells me where you sit. It does not tell me why I should remember you. The second mistake is the brochure: a long list of adjectives, a fast, flexible, innovative, customer-focused team. Nobody talks like that, and I stop listening after the third adjective. The third mistake is the big ask. Can we have a meeting with your whole team next month? Probably not. The people I remember start with one result, tell me in one sentence what they do differently, and ask for something small. Can I send you one page by email? Yes, of course you can.

I wrote my first pitch the night before a regional meeting in Miami. It was almost three minutes long, and it was my whole career, from my first job as a sales representative. Nobody stopped me, because people are polite, but nobody asked me a question either. For the second version, I cut it to one minute and I started with a result: we doubled the number of clinics in two years. That was better, people looked at me. But I had six numbers in that minute, and later nobody remembered any of them. The third version had one number, one sentence about my team, and one small ask. I stopped asking for a big meeting. I asked for a short call, fifteen minutes, the next week. Four directors said yes. The lesson for me was simple. A pitch is not a summary of everything you have done. It is the reason for the next conversation.
